correctness.rationale:
The theorem is proved from the recursive definition of \(h\), an inductive least-height lemma, Legendre valuations, and lcm prime powers. For each \(k\ge3\), the power-of-two threshold \(B=E_{k-1}\) obeys \(
u_2((B+1)!)=B-1\) and \(
u_2((B+2)!)=B\), while each other factorial valuation is at most the binary one. For lcms, \(
u_p(L(N))=\lfloor\log_p Nfloor\) gives the exact plateau. At twice its threshold, the odd-height obstruction gives upper \(k-1\), and a prime of lcm exponent \(a=E_{k-2}\) gives lower \(k-1\); the prime is explicit at levels three and four, and guaranteed by Bertrand for all higher levels. The initial levels are handled separately, and finite regression does not replace proof.

value.rationale: The factorials and initial-interval lcms are fundamental arithmetic sequences against which to test prime-tower height; unlike the unrestricted least-height number, their first hitting behavior is not automatic. The all-level \(F_k/G_k\) laws contrast two distinct growth scales, and exact lcm-height plateaux of length \(E_k\) followed by drops at 2E_k reveal a non-monotone structural phenomenon at arbitrarily high levels. This identifies natural boundaries and a prime-existence mechanism, not a fixed-size example or arbitrary parameter slice.
